messages.author: 97d82fedb7016adb
messages.subject: speedup tip for binomial_logit
parts:
Hi there!

I am analyzing a (large) data-set where I am experiencing speed "problems". The measurement per observation is a 0 to 100 count variable. I am trying now to model this type of data with the binomial_logit(100, Lodds) distribution in Stan. Lodds does represent my predicted mean log-odds.

In an earlier iteration of the model I used some transform of the original count data and then used a normal distribution on the transformed data. This "normal-transformed" model was already slow for my data set (per chain 55h). The binomial_logit seems to model the data better, but is unfortunately a lot slower as it looks like - I did not yet use the full data-set, smaller runs show already quite a drastic increase in running time.

Any suggestions on how to speed this up?

Should I again transform the original data to the logit scale, i.e. model instead of the count c this:

logit(c/100) ~ normal(Lodds, XXX)

but what is XXX then?

Any hints of how to speed this model would be great.

Many thanks!

Best,
Sebastian

messages.author: 97d82fedb7016adb
messages.subject: Re: speedup tip for binomial_logit
parts:
Hi!
 
To answer the question for the sample logit myself: XXX, the standard deviation of the sample logit, is by means of the delta method roughly sqrt(1/(N*p(1-p))) with p=inv_logit(Lodds).
 
Still, the question remains if it is really worth doing all these computations in order to replace a binomial_logit sampling satement with a normal sampling statement. The latter I am only doing for speed reasons.
 
Any experience here would be very welcome.
 
Many thanks and best regards,
 
Sebastian

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] speedup tip for binomial_logit
parts:
I'm not sure why binomial_logit would be a lot slower
than the normal. Could you share the rest of your model?

The normal is particularly easy to evaluate with fixed deviation
on the log scale --- it's just subtraction and multiplications/division.

I'd think the normal would be a good approximation with counts of
100 if the success probability isn't too close to 0 or 1.
You can just fit the deviation --- that would give you the equivalent
of overdispersion in the binomial. You need to be careful with
logit(1) and logit(0) as they produce +inf and -inf.

There's also the Poisson approximation to large
binomials and negative binomial for overdispersion.

- Bob

Fitting the deviation is not so straightforward - the standard-deviation is not constant in the binomial setting (p=0.5 has largest sd).
 
Anyway, I take from you post, that it is actually worth a try to switch to normal for speed reasons... and since 100 possible events is fairly large, the normal approximations should work, could well be true.
 
Best,
Sebastian
